articles.title: ‘Preparation is important’: Abhishek Sharma explains how he stays ahead of opposition bowlers
articles.summary: INDORE: Abhishek Sharma likes to do \"uncomfortable\" things during practice sessions.
articles.body: INDORE: Abhishek Sharma likes to do "uncomfortable" things during practice sessions. He believes that such preparation keeps him battle-ready and ensures he is not caught by "surprise" when facing world-class bowlers.With Roston Chase having dismissed the left-hander twice earlier in the series, and Abhishek's weakness against off-spinners well documented, West Indies began with the 34-year-old offie in an attempt to counter him from the word go.The 26-year-old knew what the visitors were trying to exploit, but this time he was ready. He bided his time, played out the first over he faced from Chase and, once settled, launched into him in the next. A 111.6 kmph faster one was smashed through the covers for four while a much slower delivery was deposited over wide long-off for six, and the dose was repeated as he struck another six over covers.Abhishek never looked back thereafter as he raced to his 14th T20I fifty and finished with a 30-ball 69. During his innings at the Holkar Stadium on Sunday, he achieved another staggering feat, scoring 72 per cent of his runs through the off-side.In the process, he became the fastest batter to score 2,000 T20I runs. He reached the landmark in just 1,024 balls, 140 fewer than the previous record holder, Suryakumar Yadav, who took 1,164 deliveries to get there.Abhishek's career strike rate stands at 195.95, and he feels the preparation he puts in behind the scenes is crucial to sustaining that approach."I think preparation is important. If I want to just continue playing like this, and that's the plan for the team, then preparation really matters. I always believe in that. It always depends on the teams and the bowlers I'm going to face. So, whenever I have time, it's (preparation) very specific... how bowlers are going to plan against me, how I'm going to execute my plan and dominate," said Abhishek."As a batter, if you have to face world-class bowlers, you have to be ready for all the plans. I always want that preparation in practice which makes me a bit uncomfortable so that I wouldn't be surprised in the match. So I always allow myself to be in that position during training," he added.West Indies allrounder Shamar Springer also lauded Abhishek's innings, which circumvented their plans and forced them to switch to a 'Plan B' that involved bowling a defensive line to him."He is a world-class player. But I guess our 'Plan B' was to just be as defensive as possible and try to make him get singles and twos. It was just a matter of trying to pull him back because there's not much control you can really have here. The wickets are so good and those players are world-class players and they're the best for a reason. So, it's not really much you can do besides be defensive," said Springer.Earlier in the year, during the T20 World Cup, Abhishek struggled against off-spinners and almost every team targeted that weakness. During that period, he would often try to force his way out of trouble.Eight months later, while Abhishek's ability to destroy attacks at the top remains intact, his willingness to wait just a little longer before launching into the opposition has made this version of him an even scarier proposition for opponents to dismantle.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Abhishek Sharma continues to redefine aggressive batting in T20 Internationals, combining an extraordinary scoring rate with the ability to find solutions when opposition bowlers try to expose his weaknesses. The India opener crossed the 2,000-run mark in T20Is during the third match against West Indies in Indore on Sunday, and former India batter Ajinkya Rahane believes his ability to adapt without compromising his attacking intent makes him a special talent.Abhishek smashed 69 off just 30 deliveries to power India to a formidable total of 223 in the third T20I, helping the hosts take a 2-1 lead in the five-match series. His innings featured explosive strokeplay, but Rahane was particularly impressed by the left-hander's approach against off-spinner Roston Chase, an area in which Abhishek has faced challenges previously.Speaking on Cricbuzz, Rahane praised the youngster's ability to find different methods of scoring runs while maintaining his trademark aggression and high strike rate."See, he's a special talent. We were talking about him, his intent every single time. What I like about Abhishek Sharma is his finding methods to score runs. If he's struggling with a particular area, he will find a way, find that different method to score runs without losing that intent, without losing that strike rate, I mean," Rahane said.Abhishek Sharma's ability to adapt impresses RahaneAbhishek's approach against Chase in Indore offered a glimpse of the adaptability Rahane highlighted. Rather than immediately taking on the off-spinner, the left-hander initially played a few deliveries cautiously before switching gears in the third over, striking two sixes and a boundary through the off-side.The adjustment allowed Abhishek to counter the challenge without abandoning his natural attacking instincts, underlining why Rahane considers his batting approach particularly impressive. Abhishek boasts a T20I strike rate of 195.95, the highest among batters who have faced at least 250 deliveries in the format.Rahane also highlighted the remarkable consistency behind the opener's aggressive style, pointing to his ability to maintain a scoring rate close to 200 across his international career."We see his strike rate throughout his career so far is close to 200. articles.title: Brydon Carse can return, says Rob Key, as England reveal central contracts
articles.summary: Director of cricket Rob Key believes Brydon Carse can play for England again, despite an ongoing investigation into an incident outside a Derby nightclub in August.
articles.body:
Director of cricket Rob Key believes Brydon Carse can play for England again, despite an ongoing investigation into an incident outside a Derby nightclub in August.

Carse was arrested then de-arrested, with Derbyshire Police subsequently taking no action over allegations of an assault. The pace bowler has since been charged by the Cricket Regulator with breaching England and Wales Cricket Board professional conduct rules.

The 31-year-old is among 39 players named in England's updated list of contracted players, announced on Monday. The two-year deal he was given last year runs until the autumn of 2027.

Carse is available for England selection but has not been part of a squad since the Derby incident as he takes time away from international cricket.

Asked if he can see a situation where the Durham man plays for England again, Key told the Test Match Special podcast: "Yeah, I can do, depending what happens with the outcome of that [the Regulator charge].

"Myself, like a lot of people who work for the ECB, you get in these jobs to make some decisions that help English cricket and you also want players to be able to maximise their potential and have great careers. You don't get in them to sit on calls about all the things that have happened off the field over the last bit.

"As far as Brydon Carse is concerned, we'll find out what happens in the near future, and there's a chance he can come back and play for England."

Mahmud takes Test hat-trick - can you name the others in past 40 years?

As well as announcing player deals, England also confirmed new-look backroom teams underneath Test head coach Stephen Fleming and white-ball counterpart Brendon McCullum.

Fleming has brought in Richard Dawson, who leaves his position as Glamorgan head coach, alongside former England wicketkeeper James Foster and South African Eric Simons. Fleming worked with both Foster and Simons at Indian Premier League side Chennai Super Kings.

Marcus Trescothick, who took interim charge of the Test team for the home series against Pakistan, remains with the red-ball team.

McCullum keeps the bulk of the staff who worked with him across formats: Sarah Taylor, Jeetan Patel and Tim Southee. Kevin Pietersen will also work with the white-ball teams in the run-up to the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa next year.

Of the 39 players handed England deals, 30 have full central contracts and nine are on development contracts.

The large number of players on England deals is a result of high-earners like Ben Stokes and Mark Wood retiring from international cricket and freeing up space in the budget.

Eleven players, including Test captain Joe Root and white-ball captain Harry Brook, are given two-year contracts.

In an unprecedented move for an uncapped player, pace bowler Henry Crocombe is also given a two-year contract.

England's centrally contracted players: Joe Root* (Yorkshire), Harry Brook* (Yorkshire), Rehan Ahmed (Leicestershire), Jofra Archer* (Sussex), Gus Atkinson* (Surrey), Sonny Baker* (Hampshire), Tom Banton (Somerset), Shoaib Bashir (Derbyshire), Jacob Bethell* (Warwickshire), Jos Buttler (Lancashire), Brydon Carse (Durham), Sam Cook (Essex), Jordan Cox* (Essex), Henry Crocombe* (Sussex/Surrey), Sam Curran* (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Ben Duckett (Nottinghamshire), Emilio Gay (Durham), Matthew Fisher (Surrey), Will Jacks* (Surrey), Dan Lawrence (Surrey), Saqib Mahmood (Lancashire), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Ollie Pope (Surrey), Matthew Potts (Durham), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Ollie Robinson (Sussex), Phil Salt (Lancashire), Jamie Smith (Surrey), Josh Tongue* (Nottinghamshire)

*Denotes two-year deal through until 30 September 2028.

England development contracted players: James Coles (Sussex), Mason Crane (Glamorgan), Josh Hull (Leicestershire), Eddie Jack (Hampshire), Ben McKinney (Durham), Liam Patterson-White (Nottinghamshire), Thomas Rew (Somerset). Matthew Revis (Yorkshire), Mitch Stanley (Lancashire).

Crocombe is one of five specialist fast bowlers to be given a multi-year deal, joining Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Sonny Baker and Josh Tongue.

Before the Derby incident, Carse had not played for England since the Ashes in January because of a wrist injury.

Prior to the injury, the Durham man was an international regular across formats and was the only England seamer to play in all five Tests in Australia.

With inexperienced bowlers like Baker and Crocombe receiving longer contracts, Key was asked if a lack of extension for Carse revealed England's feelings on his international future.

"No," replied the former Kent batter. "I think it means if he gets a chance to come back and play for England he's got to try to maximise his career and be the best bowler he possibly can be.

"That investigation is going on with the Regulator. I don't know a lot about what happens in that investigation, because that is with them and we deal with that afterwards. There's nothing really I can say about that. We haven't had those conversations. We'll find out more in due course. We'll find out more when that investigation comes to a head."

Along with Crocombe, Emilio Gay, Jordan Cox, Dan Lawrence, Tom Banton, Sam Cook and Matt Fisher are given full central contracts for the first time.

Ollie Robinson returns to the contract list after missing out for the past two years, rewarded following his superb return to the Test team in the home summer.

Off-spinner Shoaib Bashir keeps his deal and is the only specialist red-ball spinner on the list. However, Mason Crane and Liam Patterson-White are given developmental deals as an indication of how England could grow their Test spin-bowling options.

articles.title: West Indies duo Rovman Powell and Sherfane Rutherford penalised for breaching ICC Code of Conduct
articles.summary: West Indies batters Rovman Powell and Sherfane Rutherford have landed in trouble with the International Cricket Council (ICC) after separate on-field
articles.body: West Indies batters Rovman Powell and Sherfane Rutherford have landed in trouble with the International Cricket Council (ICC) after separate on-field incidents during the second T20I against India in Ranchi on Friday. Both players have received official reprimands and one demerit point each for breaching the ICC Code of Conduct during the match.Why were Rovman Powell and Sherfane Rutherford reprimanded?Powell was found guilty of breaching Article 2.2 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which deals with the abuse of cricket equipment, clothing, ground equipment or fixtures and fittings.The incident occurred in the sixth over of the West Indies innings after Powell was dismissed by Mayank Yadav. Following his dismissal, the West Indies batter struck the ball away with his bat, prompting the disciplinary action.Rutherford, meanwhile, breached Article 2.8 of the ICC Code of Conduct, which relates to showing dissent at an umpire's decision during the second T20I. The incident took place in the 13th over of the innings when Rutherford aggressively shouted at the umpire after a delivery he believed was wide was ruled legitimate.Both players accept sanctionsBoth Powell and Rutherford admitted their respective offences and accepted the sanctions proposed by match referee Prakash Bhatt of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees. As a result, no formal hearings were required.The charges were levelled by on-field umpires Jayaraman Madanagopal and Rohan Pandit, third umpire Nitin Menon, and fourth umpire Virender Sharma. The one demerit point awarded to each player has been added to their disciplinary records. Since both incidents were their first offences in the preceding 24 months, neither player had any previous demerit points recorded during that period.What are the ICC's penalties for Level 1 offences?According to the ICC Code of Conduct, Level 1 breaches carry a minimum penalty of an official reprimand and a maximum penalty of a fine of 50 per cent of a player's match fee. Players can also receive one or two demerit points, depending on the nature and severity of the offence.Demerit points remain on a player's disciplinary record for 24 months from the date of the offence. A total of 39 players are now under contract with Ollie Robinson, uncapped fellow seamer Henry Crocombe and Crawley's replacement as opener in the Test side, Emilio Gay , among eight previously uncontracted players to be rewarded with full deals.

They join batters Jordan Cox, Dan Lawrence and Tom Banton and pacemen Sam Cook and Matthew Fisher , with all but Robinson - who had a deal in 2022 and 2023 - handed contracts for the first time.

Cox, who has become an important player across formats, and Crocombe, who could debut during this month's ODI tri-series in Pakistan, have signed two-year agreements until September 30, 2028, with the latter the first England player to pen a multi-year deal before making an international appearance.

Surrey-bound seamer Crocombe came to wider attention earlier this season when he took back-to-back hat-tricks for Sussex in the County Championship against Somerset and Essex on his way to bagging 40 wickets at an average of 23.52.

Eleven players all told are under contract until autumn 2028, including Test captain Joe Root, white-ball skipper Harry Brook and seamers Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue.

The deals of Jacob Bethell, Sam Curran, Will Jacks and Sonny Baker also run until then, with Hampshire quick Baker upgraded to a two-year deal after a strong summer.

Batter Ben Duckett and wicketkeeper Jamie Smith's deals expire in 2027 and when asked why they were not presented with two-year contracts, England managing director of men's cricket Rob Key said: "We feel this is the best thing that gets the best out of those guys."

Carse still under contract; teenager Rew awarded development deal

Seamer Brydon Carse , who has not played for England since an incident outside a Derby nightclub in August that saw him briefly arrested, remains contracted until the end of September 2027 having penned a two-year deal last autumn.

Former captain Ben Stokes and fast bowler Mark Wood's contracts have finished following their international retirements.

Nine development deals have been given out, to James Coles, Mason Crane, Josh Hull, Eddie Jack, Ben McKinney, Liam Patterson-White, Thomas Rew, Matthew Revis and Mitch Stanley.

Glamorgan leg-spinner Crane could make his first England appearance in over eight years in the upcoming tri-series in the subcontinent that also includes Sri Lanka.

Somerset wicketkeeper-batter Rew, 18 - whose older brother James played a Test against New Zealand in 2026 - is the youngest player on the contract list.

England keep faith with Pope and Bashir but Crawley ignored

Batter Pope has not played for England since being dropped for Jacob Bethell after the third Ashes Test last winter having averaged 20.83 in the series to that point, but was included in squads for the 3-0 Test rout at home to Pakistan this summer.

Off-spinner Bashir has also been handed a fresh contract despite appearing in only two Tests in the last year, both against New Zealand in June.

He did not feature at all during the 4-1 Ashes thrashing in Australia with all-rounder Jacks preferred as the spin option, while he sat out the Pakistan series as part-time spinner Lawrence earned the nod to support the four-pronged pack attack due to his batting ability.

All-rounder Rehan Ahmed , who lost his place in the ODI squad for this month's tri-series in Pakistan , is given new terms, too, with Crawley and left-arm seamer Luke Wood the only senior players whose deals were due to elapse not awarded an extension.

Surrey's seam-bowling all-rounder Tom Lawes was on a development deal for 2025-26, which has not been renewed.

Crawley was dropped after averaging 27.30 during The Ashes, while white-ball specialist Wood has not featured since a T20 international against India at Chester-le-Street in July.

Robinson, Cox, Gay among those to earn contracts

Robinson made a triumphant return to international cricket this summer after over two years in exile, picking up 28 wickets in four Tests against New Zealand and Pakistan at an average below 10, claiming two five-fors and a best of 5-39.

Batters Cox, Gay and Lawrence also helped England sweep Pakistan, while Cox and Banton were then part of T20 and one-day international series wins over Sri Lanka in September.

Cox hit fifties in all three Tests against Pakistan after stepping in for the injured Bethell at No 3, while his maiden ODI half-century came versus Sri Lanka in the series decider as he deputised for Jos Buttler following the former captain's hamstring strain.

Banton - who was also involved in the 4-0 T20I thrashing of India in July - scored his first international hundred against Sri Lanka in the final ODI at The Kia Oval, having struck 73 in the previous game and also an unbeaten fifty in the second T20I between the sides.

Lawrence, like Cox, contributed three Test fifties against Pakistan after replacing Stokes in the XI, while opener Gay has three half-centuries in six Tests since taking the axed Crawley's spot, firstly against New Zealand at Lord's in June.

One of Cox, Gay and Lawrence may have to miss out on the Test XI in South Africa this winter with Bethell with set to return.

Carse faced no punishment after a police investigation following the Derby incident but was then charged by the Cricket Regulator for breaching conduct regulations.

The Durham quick, who has played county cricket since the incident, remains available for England selection.

It is understood decisions around his involvement are being taken on a tour-by-tour basis.

Key said on Monday of Carse, who was England's leading wicket-taker during the Ashes drubbing with 22 scalps: "I don't see, at the moment, anything to suggest he won't continue on that contract, but we will find out more as it goes on.

"We feel Brydon just needs to get his house in order. Once all this is dealt with, we will decide if he can play international cricket again."

Simons to join England Test coaching staff

England also announced an update to their coaching staff with former South Africa international Eric Simons joining Fleming's Test group for the South Africa tour, having previously worked with the New Zealander at IPL side Chennai Super Kings.

Simons, 64, played 23 one-day internationals for the Proteas between 1994 and 1995.

Marcus Trescothick remains part of the red-ball backroom team, with Richard Dawson - the ECB's new lead spin-bowling coach after leaving his job as Glamorgan head coach - and ex-England and Essex wicketkeeper James Foster also involved.

Brendon McCullum's white-ball coaching group, starting with November's tour of Australia, will include ex-England Women wicketkeeper Sarah Taylor, who worked across formats this summer and was credited with improving Smith's glovework.

McCullum's fellow New Zealanders Jeetan Patel and Tim Southee will also be involved in 50-over and T20 cricket, as will former England batter Kevin Pietersen, who began his specialist mentor role against Sri Lanka recently in a deal that runs up to and including the 2027 ODI World Cup.

Elsewhere, former Sussex and England spin-bowling all-rounder Michael Yardy has been named elite national batting lead.

Key on coaching staff: 'We have best of what this country has to offer'

Key said on the coaching changes: "I believe when you take on a role as England head coach, you should have the team around you that you think can deliver that success.

"We now have two set-ups that will really enhance all the careers of the players they come in contact with.

"Along with Jonathan Trott doing the Lions, we have the best of what this country has to offer - up-and-coming coaches as well. That is part of a succession plan that may or may not happen.

"I think a number of coaches have the potential to not only learn but go and do the [head coach] job in the future.

"Dawson would be near the top of that list. He is someone that [Fleming] was really keen to try and get to come and do this job. I think it's brilliant and our gain is Glamorgan's loss."

Key is hopeful Dawson's new position leading the spin-bowling department can boost the number and quality of slow bowlers in England but says "that is not an easy problem to solve."

articles.title: Tushar Deshpande's hat-trick, five-wicket haul put Mumbai in command against Chandigarh in Ranji Trophy
articles.summary: MUMBAI: On a mission to prove a point after being ignored from the India ‘A’ touring party for the upcoming New Zealand tour, paceman Tushar Deshpande,
articles.body: MUMBAI: On a mission to prove a point after being ignored from the India ‘A’ touring party for the upcoming New Zealand tour, paceman Tushar Deshpande, playing in his landmark 50th first-class match, turned on the heat in steamy conditions in Chandigarh, producing a fiery opening burst of five for 17 in seven overs, including a hat-trick, to shoot out the visitors for a mere 78 in 19.1 overs in reply to Mumbai’s 429 on Day Two of their Ranji Trophy Elite Group D match at the Wankhede Stadium.Sprinting in during twilight after his exploits helped Mumbai enforce the follow-on, Deshpande cleaned up the stumps of Vishu Kashyap with another scorching incoming delivery for a three-ball duck in the only over that he and Mumbai bowled, leaving Chandigarh, enduring a nightmare, limping at 0 for one.Joining in the fun against Chandigarh’s mediocre batting, seamer Mohit Avasthi took three for nine in six overs, as Mumbai logged a humongous 351-run first-innings lead. On Tuesday morning, the hosts would be looking to wrap up this farcical game with a bonus-point win. Looking like lambs to the slaughter, Chandigarh, who started playing domestic cricket only in 2018-19 after the Lodha reforms kicked in, folded up for their lowest total in first-class cricket.After he had Chandigarh opener Arsalan Khan (2, 20b) chopping a ball onto his stumps in the seventh over, Deshpande walked into the history books in style in the 11th over when he took the wickets of Arjun Azad (20, top-edged a hook to Sylivester D’Souza at long leg), Shivam Bhambri (0, 1b, bowled by a pacy leg-cutter) and Deepinder Kush (caught by Yashasvi Jaiswal at first slip) to become the sixth Mumbai bowler to take a hat-trick in first-class cricket.Jahangir Khot, Umesh Kulkarni, Abdul Ismail, Royston Dias and Shardul Thakur (against Meghalaya at BKC in the 2025-26 season) are the other Mumbai bowlers to have taken a first-class hat-trick for Mumbai.It took just 20 balls for Deshpande to record his sixth five-wicket haul when he trapped Chandigarh all-rounder Raj Angad Bawa lbw for a four-ball duck. Floored by Deshpande’s strikes, Chandigarh collapsed like a pack of cards, losing five wickets for four runs to slide from 25 for one in the 11th over to 29 for six in the 13th over. Earlier in the day, the 31-year-old fast bowler had chipped in with an entertaining 44 (47b, 4x4, 2x6).Meanwhile, Mumbai vice-captain Ayush Mhatre did not come out to field, with Suved Parkar substituting for him.Earlier, as has been the case in the last five seasons or so, Mumbai’s last five batters virtually outscored the first five batters comfortably.Resuming at their overnight score of 249 for five, Mumbai lost skipper Siddhesh Lad (86, 192b, 9x4) and Shams Mulani (39, 68b, 4x4, 1x6) on Monday with not much added to the total. However, rising to the occasion yet again, Mumbai’s lower-order batters Tanush Kotian (58, 91b, 5x4), seamer Mohit Avasthi (56 not out, 119b, 6x4, 2x6), who scored his fourth first-class half-century, and Deshpande made valuable contributions to help Mumbai post 429 in a marathon batting effort of 136.5 overs. The trio helped Mumbai add 180 to their total on Monday while keeping Chandigarh on the field for two sessions.For Chandigarh, medium-pacers Raj Angad Bawa — who was part of India’s Under-19 World Cup-winning team in the West Indies — and Rohit Dhanda were the most successful bowlers, taking eight wickets between themselves. After going wicketless on Day One, Bawa took four for 73 in 21.5 overs, while Dhanda had figures of four for 78 in 26 overs.The 23-year-old Bawa took all three Mumbai wickets that fell in the first session. After adding 74 in 126 balls for the sixth wicket with Mulani, Lad fell 14 runs short of his century, bowled by an incoming ball. Mulani was caught down the leg side by wicketkeeper A Rana, as Mumbai were reduced to 271 for seven.However, coming off a match-saving half-century of 52 in the second multi-day match for India ‘A’ against Australia ‘A’ in Pondicherry, Deshpande produced some fireworks, putting on a 71-run partnership with Kotian for the eighth wicket in just 83 balls.Deshpande was caught at second slip by Shivam Bhambri off Bawa.Showing that he’s no mug with the bat, Avasthi, together with Kotian, stretched Mumbai’s total with their 67-run stand in 146 balls for the ninth wicket, which left the tiring Chandigarh bowlers completely deflated in the severe heat.Kotian reached his 19th half-century in 77 balls, with a single to mid-on off Vishu Kashyap.Mohit reached his fifty with a flicked four off Raj Bawa to deep mid-wicket, consuming 109 balls.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Kevin Pietersen set to stay white-ball-only mentor for England - but could still impact Ashes batters, says Rob Key
articles.summary: Rob Key on England white-ball mentor Kevin Pietersen: "There is no one better breaking down batting, talking technically but more importantly how you score runs", England MD says people must "respect" former Test captain Ben Stokes' decision to retire from international cricket
articles.body:
Pietersen began a specialist mentor role with Brendon McCullum's limited-overs outfit during the T20 and ODI series wins over Sri Lanka in September, with that running until the end of the next 50-over World Cup in Africa at the end of 2027.

However, with many of England's Test batters also key parts of the white-ball set-up, including Joe Root, Harry Brook and Jacob Bethell, men's managing director of cricket Key says players will inevitably pick Pietersen's brains about the longest form.

The 46-year-old's haul of 13,797 international runs included 1,181 in 104 Tests with 23 hundreds and 35 further half-centuries.

The 2027 Ashes begins at Trent Bridge on June 18 next year.

'There is no one better breaking down batting than KP'

Speaking to Sky Sports News , on the day England announced their central-contract list and some coaching updates , Key said of Pietersen's position: "At the moment, I think it's just white-ball cricket but there are a lot of players that are multi-format players.

"Our best players are the best players across formats. That doesn't mean they haven't already started talking about Test cricket, talking about batting in general.

"Pietersen has been outstanding. There is no one better breaking down batting, talking technically but more importantly how you score runs.

"KP was one of the best we ever had and one of the best to talk about it, so they are incredibly lucky to have someone like that.

"He is someone who has a lot of options - he could go off and do other things and make a lot more money actually.

"He is doing this job because he wants to give back to English cricket and loves what he's doing."

Pietersen will not be with England during this month's ODI tri-series in the subcontinent, in which McCullum's men will play Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

He will return for the five T20s and three ODIs in Australia in November.

Any chance of Stokes returning to play for England?

England will lock horns with Australia again in Melbourne in March for the 150th anniversary Test before welcoming their rivals for the Ashes in the summer.

Key does not expect former Test captain Ben Stokes to be involved having retired from international cricket in June but when asked whether any "bridges had been burned, he replied: "Not as far as I am concerned.

"[New Test coach] Stephen Fleming spoke to [Stokes] and he was pretty adamant about the fact he was pretty happy with his decision.

"Only Stokes knows what it was like to play 100-plus Tests and go through the scrutiny of a 10-plus-year career, where he has done so much for English cricket.

"I look back on the last four years and I have loved nearly every minute and I think we just have to respect his decision."

articles.title: Afghanistan Premier League: Ollie Pope withdraws from draft
articles.summary: England batter Ollie Pope pulls out of the draft for the Afghanistan Premier League.
articles.body:
England batter Ollie Pope has pulled out of the draft for the Afghanistan Premier League.

Pope had been due to be the only centrally contracted England player in the running for the inaugural edition of the APL, which is set to take place in the United Arab Emirates later this year.

On Monday, when England's latest batch of contracts were confirmed, director of cricket Rob Key said he would not play in the APL but it is "legally hard" to prevent England players from taking part.

In order for any English player to take part in the league they would require a No Objection Certificate from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB).

With batter Pope being a contracted player, Key would have been involved in deciding the Surrey man's availability for the APL.

However, it is understood Pope has taken the decision to withdraw from the draft taking place later this month independently of Key's view on the competition.

"Legally it is hard to stop players going over and playing in these competitions," Key told the Test Match Special podcast. "It becomes a moral judgement and players have to be prepared to take the right moral stance.

"Personally, and it is easy for me to say, I would not go and play. But it is down to the player to make that decision."

How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal

The ECB has refused to schedule bilateral cricket with Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in the country in 2021.

Last year, ECB chair Richard Thompson described the Taliban's oppression of women and girls as "gender apartheid".

England have, however, continued to play against Afghanistan at global events, including World Cups in both limited-overs formats and the Champions Trophy.

"I don't agree with the way women have been treated in Afghanistan," said Key. "The way things happen out there is not something I agree with so it is not something I would go and do."

Pope has been handed a new 12-month England contract despite not playing international cricket since the third Ashes Test in Australia last December.

He was recalled to the Test squad for the series against Pakistan in the home summer and has stood in as captain on six occasions, including against India at The Oval in 2025.

When asked if he had made his feelings clear to Pope, Key replied: "I had that conversation and Ollie will have to make his decision."

Before England's last meeting with Afghanistan, at the 2025 Champions Trophy, Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi led calls for the fixture to be boycotted.

In September, she told BBC Sport: "Why are we here again? Women and girls in Afghanistan are denied the same rights as those in our country, and the women's team lives in exile," she said.

"Does that not concern the players, especially those with daughters, sisters or mothers?

"I hope the International Cricket Council (ICC) refuses to sanction this event. Continuing to allow Afghanistan full member status makes a mockery of its own membership criteria."

Former England batter Dawid Malan is entered into the APL draft, alongside the likes of Moeen Ali, James Vince and James Rew – Somerset's Rew made his Test debut in June.

"As players we take our guidance from the ICC and the boards," Malan told the TMS podcast.

"As a player it is tough because you have what is morally right and what is by the law. I have a daughter and I want her to play sport and get into sport and enjoy it. I fully understand the argument, but at the end of the day I am a cricketer and need to be able to pay my rent and be able to earn a living while I can.

"England don't play bilateral series against Afghanistan, but they do play them in World Cups – what's the difference? As players, you sometimes want a board decision to be made that says 'we don't think this is right, we are making a stance against it', then the players will buy into it.

"I don't think anyone agrees with what is happening in Afghanistan, but once something gets approved you sit there as players and say: 'It's a job, and I have to play and do what I need to do', then you're stuck in a position of what is morally right and what is morally not."

On Friday, Dean Ahmad, an agent who represents ex-England all-rounder Moeen, wrote on X: "Morality in sport matters, but so does consistency.

"The Taliban's treatment of women is indefensible. Yet why are cricketers singled out while governments and corporations maintain ties with states accused of serious human rights abuses. Selective outrage isn't morality."
